name: Risk Mitigation
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: From Finding to Fixing: Turning Risk Themes into Action
lesson.summary: Risk mitigation is the follow-on work of converting identified risks and risk themes into concrete architectural changes, and it deliberately happens after an ATAM evaluation rather than during it.
lesson.body:
An ATAM evaluation is designed to produce a clear, specific list of risks, non-risks, sensitivity points, and tradeoff points, not to redesign the architecture on the spot. Risk mitigation is the work that follows, where the stakeholders and architects who received that list decide what to actually do about each risk and each risk theme. Keeping mitigation as a separate, later step is intentional: an evaluation that spends its limited workshop time debating fixes instead of finding risks will surface fewer risks overall, and the fixes proposed under time pressure, in the middle of a workshop, are rarely the best ones available.

Mitigation for an individual risk usually maps fairly directly onto the decision that created it. The lending protocol relying on a single exchange's price pool, identified earlier as a manipulation risk, can be mitigated by switching to an oracle network that aggregates prices from multiple independent sources and rejects a price update that moves too far from a recent time weighted average in a single block. Both changes directly address the mechanism the risk statement named: a single, quickly moved data source, rather than a general appeal to be more careful.

Mitigating a risk theme is harder, because a theme by definition points at a pattern rather than a single decision. The Layer 2 network whose theme was centralization creeping back in at every convenience point cannot mitigate that theme by patching one bridge contract; it needs an organizational commitment, for instance a standing rule that no new subsystem ships with a trust assumption weaker than the base layer without an explicit, documented exception and a plan to remove it. Mitigating a theme is as much a governance decision, tying back to how the project makes and enforces collective choices, as it is a technical one.

Not every identified risk gets mitigated immediately, or ever, and that is a legitimate outcome. Mitigation has costs: an oracle aggregation service adds complexity and latency, a stricter multi-signature threshold slows emergency response. Risk mitigation done well involves the stakeholders weighing the cost of the fix against the cost of the risk materializing, using the same importance and difficulty ratings the utility tree already established, and documenting the decision either way so a future review does not have to rediscover the same risk from scratch.

A mitigation that quietly introduces a new risk, common when a fix is rushed, deserves the same scrutiny the original risk received. Adding a centralized fallback oracle to cover the case where the decentralized one lags is a reasonable mitigation, but only if the review also checks what happens if that fallback itself becomes the single point of failure the rest of the architecture was trying to avoid.
